findings.title: Team administrators and owners are incorrectly denied access
findings.body: The authorization check requires a user to be both a team admin and a team owner (`isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)`). Those roles are distinct, so a team admin or owner who is not the booking organizer/attendee will be rejected even though the UI and variable name indicate either role should be permitted. Use an OR check (or the existing team-admin-or-owner authorization helper) so either authorized role can add guests.

findings.title: Guest addresses are neither normalized nor deduplicated on the server
findings.body: The API schema permits duplicate email addresses and this filter only excludes addresses already present on the booking; it does not deduplicate `guests` itself and compares addresses case-sensitively. A direct API caller can submit the same address repeatedly (or an existing/blacklisted address with different casing). Depending on the attendee database constraint this either creates duplicate attendees or makes the whole mutation fail, and casing can bypass the blacklist or create a second representation of the same mailbox. Normalize addresses and deduplicate them server-side before checking existing attendees, the blacklist, and `createMany`.

findings.title: Database attendees are committed before the calendar update succeeds
findings.body: New attendee rows are written before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` is called. If the calendar provider update fails, the mutation returns an error but the booking already contains the new guests; they receive no notifications and are absent from the external calendar. A retry may then reject them as existing, leaving the booking and calendar permanently out of sync. Handle/compensate for calendar failures or arrange the workflow so a failed external update does not leave silently committed attendee data.

findings.title: Attendee-initiated updates use the attendee's calendar credentials instead of the organizer's
findings.body: The endpoint explicitly authorizes an existing attendee to add guests, but constructs `EventManager` using `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`. For an attendee request those credentials belong to the attendee, not the booking organizer whose destination calendar and event references need updating. The handler already loads `booking.user.credentials` but does not use them. Consequently attendee-added guests commonly fail to update the organizer calendar (or attempt an update with an unrelated account); construct the manager with the booking organizer's credentials for this operation.

findings.title: Email classification uses unfiltered requested guests rather than guests actually added
findings.body: Only `uniqueGuests` are persisted, but email sending receives the original `guests` array. For example, when a request contains one existing attendee and one new address, no row is created for the existing attendee, yet `sendAddGuestsEmails` treats that attendee as a newly added guest and sends them an `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a booking confirmation) rather than the guests-added update. Pass the actual added addresses (`uniqueGuests`, after normalization) to the mailer.

findings.title: The mutation permits adding attendees to cancelled or rejected bookings
findings.body: After locating and authorizing the booking, the handler does not validate its status or whether it is still actionable. A caller can invoke this authenticated endpoint directly for a cancelled or rejected booking, creating attendee rows, updating the calendar, and emailing attendees that guests were added to an event that is no longer occurring. Reject non-active booking statuses (and define the intended past-event policy) before modifying attendees.
